query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under rapid heating/cooling conditions, the extent of atomic diffusion during a short, controlled dwell time at the synthesis temperature governs whether noble metal-based HEA nanoparticles transform from a disordered, kinetically trapped state into a thermodynamically favored, single‐phase ordered solid solution. Insufficient dwell time limits the necessary atomic rearrangements, resulting in phase separation or elemental segregation, whereas an excessively long dwell promotes overgrowth and decomposition. Moreover, the controlled dwell facilitates sluggish diffusion that promotes the disorder-to-order transition.
generation.material_initial_state: Disordered, solid‐solution HEA nanoparticles produced by ultrafast Joule-heating from a mixed noble metal salt precursor.
generation.intervention: Introduce and vary a controlled dwell period at the synthesis temperature (as reported in the cited studies) following initial ultrafast heating and prior to rapid cooling, while keeping all other parameters (composition, heating/cooling rates) constant.
generation.conditions: Applicable to multi-element noble metal systems synthesized under extreme heating and cooling conditions, with a synthesis temperature near that reported in the evidence where atomic mobility is limited.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of atomic diffusion/rearrangement during the dwell period that enables a disorder-to-order transition.
generation.mechanism: A delicate balance exists wherein a brief dwell allows sufficient atomic mobility for the thermodynamic drive to lower the free energy by achieving an ordered, single-phase state, but too short a dwell traps the precursor in a metastable, disordered state that can lead to phase separation, while too long a dwell promotes particle growth and segregation. This transition is underpinned by the inherently sluggish diffusion characteristic of multi-principal-element alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Using an optimally tuned dwell time will yield uniform, nanoscale HEA nanoparticles with the targeted single-phase ordered (e.g., L10 intermetallic) structure and controlled morphology, while deviations (either too short or too long dwell) will lead to observable phase splitting, elemental segregation, or uncontrolled growth relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized by ultrafast Joule-heating without a deliberately controlled dwell period at the synthesis temperature, typically resulting in a disordered solid-solution state.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies for noble metal-based HEA systems under kinetic trapping regimes (rapid heating/cooling, ~1100 K synthesis temperature) and may not hold if synthesis conditions are significantly altered (e.g., lower temperatures, slower cooling rates, or in solution-based systems with higher atomic mobility).
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal dwell time and the quantitative changes in ordering versus phase separation require further determination and likely depend on the specific elemental combinations and exact thermal profile.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of nanoparticles from an identical multi-noble metal precursor under constant rapid heating and cooling conditions while varying only the dwell time at ~1100 K over a broad range. Use characterization tools to assess crystal structure, elemental distribution, and particle size.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to determine phase purity and detect any phase splitting or ordering transitions
High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) for particle size and morphology analysis
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping for assessing elemental segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If systematic variation of the dwell time does not correlate with changes in the crystal structure (i.e., if all samples, regardless of dwell time, exhibit the same disordered or ordered phase with no trend in phase purity or morphology), then the hypothesis that the dwell time controls the disorder-to-order transition is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures. It is demonstrated that the formation of HEA nanoparticles is governed by stochastic principles and the inhibition of precursor mobility during the formation process favors the formation of a single phase. The proposed formation principle is supported by simulations of the nanoparticle formation

Synthesizing multi-principal element intermetallic (MPEI; more than three elements) nanoparticles requires fine control of the reaction conditions, which has been difficult to achieve by traditional synthesis methods () (e.g., furnace annealing) because of the slow heating/cooling rates. Specifically, the long heating durations of annealing-based techniques cause particle growth and agglomeration, preventing the synthesis of nanoscale MPEIs. An added complication is the thermodynamic immiscibility of the constituent elements, which results in phase separation (fig. S1) (, ). While phase separation can be circumvented by recently developed kinetic trapping techniques (), the resulting multimetallic nanoparticles are disordered solid-solution alloys [i.e., high-entropy alloys (HEAs)] () rather than ordered MPEI nanoparticles. As MPEI nanoparticles are projected to offer unique properties in catalysis (, ), there is a clear need for a new synthetic approach that can achieve nanoscale MPEI materials.

To synthesize the MPEI nanoparticles, we preloaded a carbon substrate with desired metal salt precursor combinations/ratios and Joule-heated (fig. S5) the materials with precise control of the temperature and heating/cooling rates by tuning the power applied to the substrate (fig. S6). The temperature profile and structural evolution of nanoparticles over time are illustrated in Fig. 2A. We first synthesize solid-solution (HEA) nanoparticles () by heating the metal precursors for tens of milliseconds at ~1100 K. This is a critical step for mixing the different elements without phase separation. A disorder-to-order phase transition is then achieved by rapidly reheating the materials to ~1100 K for an additional ~5 min—a limited amount of time that is sufficient to complete the desired transition from the disordered HEA structure to the ordered, single-phase MPEI configuration while simultaneously avoiding nanoparticle growth/agglomeration. Last, the single-phase MPEI structure and small particle size (~5 nm) is preserved by rapidly cooling the materials (~104 K/s).
